content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has developed the National Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), which is designed to provide structured lifestyle change programs aimed at delaying or preventing the onset of type 2 diabetes. These programs focus on evidence-based strategies to reduce diabetes risk through sustainable behavioral modifications. Programs such as the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program (MDPP) offer behavioral counseling services specifically targeting individuals who are overweight and at high risk for developing diabetes. Eligibility for MDPP coverage requires a body mass index (BMI) of at least 25 kg/m², or 23 kg/m² for Asian Americans, ensuring that individuals at significant risk receive appropriate interventions tailored to their needs. Despite the availability of these programs, access remains a challenge for some individuals due to barriers such as geographic location and financial constraints. These obstacles can limit the reach and impact of diabetes prevention efforts, particularly in underserved populations. Efforts to expand Medicare and Medicaid coverage for diabetes prevention programs have demonstrated potential in improving accessibility. Additionally, involving registered dietitian nutritionists (RDNs) and community health workers in the delivery of these programs has been shown to enhance both their accessibility and overall effectiveness, ensuring that more individuals can benefit from these critical preventive measures.
